claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Qian et al., 2020 and Zhou et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Stringent lineage-tracing strategies have revealed that neither quiescent nor reactive astrocytes convert to DANs upon PTBP1 depletion in the SNc or striatum.
claims.source: However, since the publication of these two studies in 2020, stringent lineage-tracing strategies have revealed that neither quiescent nor reactive astrocytes convert to DANs upon PTBP1 depletion in the SNc or striatum (Chen et al., 2022; Hoang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021), fueling widespread debate about the origin of these de novo generated cells and their ability to alleviate motor deficits in PD mice (Arenas, 2020; Jiang et al., 2021; Qian et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2022; Hoang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Adenine base editors (ABEs) enable gene editing independent of DNA double-strand break formation.
claims.source: In this study, we employed adenine base editors (ABEs), which enable gene editing independent of DNA double-strand break formation (Gaudelli et al., 2017) and thus without the risk of inducing chromosomal rearrangements, translocations, or large deletions (Adikusuma et al., 2018; Kosicki et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2017), to install a loss-of-function splice mutation in the Ptbp1 gene in astrocytes or neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gaudelli et al., 2017.

claims.claim: ABEs do not carry the risk of inducing chromosomal rearrangements, translocations, or large deletions.
claims.source: In this study, we employed adenine base editors (ABEs), which enable gene editing independent of DNA double-strand break formation (Gaudelli et al., 2017) and thus without the risk of inducing chromosomal rearrangements, translocations, or large deletions (Adikusuma et al., 2018; Kosicki et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2017), to install a loss-of-function splice mutation in the Ptbp1 gene in astrocytes or neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Adikusuma et al., 2018; Kosicki et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 in the SNc and striatum improves forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations in a chemically-induced PD mouse model.
claims.source: Using a chemically-induced PD mouse model, we show that downregulation of neuronal rather than astroglial PTBP1 in the SNc and striatum improves forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 induced expression of TH in non-dividing neurons of the striatum.
claims.source: Histological analysis revealed that downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 induced expression of TH, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of dopamine and other catecholamines and thus a characteristic marker of DANs, in non-dividing neurons of the striatum.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and BrdU labeling data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: TH is the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of dopamine and other catecholamines.
claims.source: Histological analysis revealed that downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 induced expression of TH, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of dopamine and other catecholamines and thus a characteristic marker of DANs, in non-dividing neurons of the striatum.
claims.evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about TH function.

claims.claim: Lack or dysfunction of TH results in dopamine deficiency and parkinsonism.
claims.source: Since lack or dysfunction of TH results in dopamine deficiency and parkinsonism, induction of TH expression in striatal neurons may explain the observed rescue of PD phenotypes in mice and provide therapeutic benefits for PD patients.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of TH in dopamine synthesis and Parkinson's disease.

claims.claim: Base editors can be applied to precisely disrupt canonical splice sites and permanently eliminate gene function in vivo.
claims.source: BEs can thus be applied to precisely disrupt canonical splice sites and permanently eliminate gene function in vivo (Kluesner et al., 2021; Musunuru et al., 2021; Rothgangl et al., 2021; Winter et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kluesner et al., 2021; Musunuru et al., 2021; Rothgangl et al., 2021; Winter et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Base editing activity was higher at splice donor sites, with the highest editing rates at the exon-intron junctions of exon 3 (92.9 ± 1.0% for SpG-ABE8e) and 7 (85.0 ± 7.2% for SpCas-ABE8e).
claims.source: In line with previous reports (Kluesner et al., 2021), base editing activity was higher at splice donor sites, with the highest editing rates at the exon-intron junctions of exon 3 (92.9 ± 1.0% for SpG-ABE8e) and 7 (85.0 ± 7.2% for SpCas-ABE8e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Average editing rates of 77% (sgRNA-ex3) and 73% (sgRNA-ex7) on genomic DNA resulted in approximately 70% and 50% reduction of Ptbp1 transcripts in Hepa cells.
claims.source: Average editing rates of 77% (sgRNA-ex3) and 73% (sgRNA-ex7) on genomic DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) resulted in approximately 70% (p<0.0004) and 50% reduction of Ptbp1 transcripts (p<0.0064) in Hepa cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), leading to a substantial reduction in PTBP1 protein levels and a significant increase in the transcription of exons known to be repressed by PTBP1 (Han et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; for sgRNA-ex3: Ptbp2, p<0.0014; Ptbp3, p<0.0051; Kcnq2, p<0.0317; for sgRNA-ex7, Ptbp2, p<0.0477; Ptbp3, p<0.0055; Kcnq2, p<0.0160).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Editing of the canonical splice donor at exon 3 generated alternative Ptbp1 splice sites in all three cell lines.
claims.source: Notably, editing of the canonical splice donor at exon 3 generated alternative Ptbp1 splice sites in all three cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which, however, did not result in functional PTBP1 protein (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Western blot data in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Alternative Ptbp1 splice sites generated by editing did not result in functional PTBP1 protein.
claims.source: Notably, editing of the canonical splice donor at exon 3 generated alternative Ptbp1 splice sites in all three cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which, however, did not result in functional PTBP1 protein (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced PTBP1 protein levels in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: 6-OHDA induced a severe unilateral lesion in the nigrostriatal pathway, characterized by an average 99% reduction in the number of TH+ DANs in the SNc ipsilateral to the injection site.
claims.source: As expected, 6-OHDA induced a severe unilateral lesion in the nigrostriatal pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), characterized by an average 99% reduction in the number of TH+ DANs in the SNc ipsilateral to the injection site (intact hemisphere: 10547 ± 2313 TH+ cells; lesioned hemisphere: 114 ± 83 TH+ cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and an average 92% decrease in fluorescence signal corresponding to striatal DA fibers (dorsal, p<0.0001; ventral, p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 6-OHDA induced an average 92% decrease in fluorescence signal corresponding to striatal DA fibers.
claims.source: As expected, 6-OHDA induced a severe unilateral lesion in the nigrostriatal pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), characterized by an average 99% reduction in the number of TH+ DANs in the SNc ipsilateral to the injection site (intact hemisphere: 10547 ± 2313 TH+ cells; lesioned hemisphere: 114 ± 83 TH+ cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and an average 92% decrease in fluorescence signal corresponding to striatal DA fibers (dorsal, p<0.0001; ventral, p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A sharp increase in activated astrocytes was observed following 6-OHDA lesion, as indicated by the upregulation of GFAP.
claims.source: In line with previous reports (Chen et al., 2022), we also observed a sharp increase in activated astrocytes, as indicated by the upregulation of the intermediate filament protein GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Chen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Ipsilateral rotations and contralateral forelimb akinesia were significantly increased following 6-OHDA lesion.
claims.source: Finally, we analyzed perturbations in spontaneous motor activities following the 6-OHDA lesion (Boix et al., 2015; Glajch et al., 2012; Iancu et al., 2005) and found that ipsilateral rotations (p=0.0012) and contralateral forelimb akinesia (P<0.0001) were significantly increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to Boix et al., 2015; Glajch et al., 2012; Iancu et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Animals treated with AAV-hsyn to downregulate PTBP1 in neurons showed a restoration of approximately 10% of TH+ cells compared to the intact hemisphere.
claims.source: When we next assessed animals treated with AAV-hsyn to downregulate PTBP1 in neurons, we observed a restoration of approximately 10% of TH+ cells compared to the intact hemisphere (intact hemisphere: 7613 ± 1386 TH+ cells; lesioned hemisphere: 721 ± 144 TH+ cells; Figure 2B and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claims.claim: Animals treated with AAV-GFAP to downregulate PTBP1 in astrocytes did not observe TH+ cells above control levels.
claims.source: In contrast, when we analyzed animals treated with AAV-GFAP to downregulate PTBP1 in astrocytes, we did not observe TH+ cells above control levels (intact hemisphere: 9209 ± 1199 TH+ cells; lesioned hemisphere: 158 ± 78 TH+ cells; Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: TH+ cells generated in the SNc upon neuronal PTBP1 downregulation did not form striatal projections.
claims.source: However, despite the presence of TH + cells in the SNc of AAV-hsyn-treated animals, we did not detect an increase in fluorescence signal corresponding to DA fibers in the striatum (ventral: AAV-GFAP, p=0.7935; AAV-hsyn, p=0.6998; dorsal: AAV-GFAP, p=0.7352; AAV-hsyn, p=0.4906), suggesting that TH+ cells generated in the SNc upon neuronal PTBP1 downregulation did not form striatal projections (Figure 2E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of striatal DA fibers shown in Figure 2E and F.

claims.claim: No differences in fluorescence intensity were detected between groups when analyzing projections of DANs in the mfb.
claims.source: Further supporting this observation, we did not detect differences in fluorescence intensity between groups when analyzing projections of DANs in the mfb (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; AAV-GFAP, p=0.3796; AAV-hsyn, p=0.2996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site was 14.7 ± 3.9% for AAV-GFAP and 15.5 ± 8.5% for AAV-hsyn in SNc tissues.
claims.source: Notably, base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site (AAV-ctrl, 0.04 ± 0.03%, AAV-GFAP, 14.7 ± 3.9%; AAV-hsyn, 15.5 ± 8.5%) as well as a reduction of Ptbp1 transcript (AAV-GFAP, 23.7 ± 12.7%, p=0.0383; AAV-hsyn, 24.8 ± 18.7%, p=0.0354) and PTBP1 protein levels (AAV-GFAP, 10.8 ± 6.3%; AAV-hsyn, 13.8 ± 10.1%) could be confirmed in SNc tissues at experimental endpoints (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Reduction of Ptbp1 transcript was 23.7 ± 12.7% for AAV-GFAP and 24.8 ± 18.7% for AAV-hsyn in SNc tissues.
claims.source: Notably, base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site (AAV-ctrl, 0.04 ± 0.03%, AAV-GFAP, 14.7 ± 3.9%; AAV-hsyn, 15.5 ± 8.5%) as well as a reduction of Ptbp1 transcript (AAV-GFAP, 23.7 ± 12.7%, p=0.0383; AAV-hsyn, 24.8 ± 18.7%, p=0.0354) and PTBP1 protein levels (AAV-GFAP, 10.8 ± 6.3%; AAV-hsyn, 13.8 ± 10.1%) could be confirmed in SNc tissues at experimental endpoints (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: 106±38 TH+ cells were found across 3 sections in the striatum of mice treated with AAV-hsyn.
claims.source: When we quantified TH+ cells in brain sections of the striatum, we found 106±38 TH+ cells across 3 sections (estimated as 2646±952 cells in the entire striatum) in mice treated with AAV-hsyn compared to no TH+ cells in the lesioned hemisphere of animals treated with AAV-ctrl (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site was 23.0 ± 6.6% in striatum tissues of AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice.
claims.source: Analysis of striatum tissues isolated from AAV-ctrl- and AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice revealed base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site (AAV-ctrl, 0.4 ± 0.1%; AAV-hsyn, 23.0 ± 6.6%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and downregulation of Ptbp1 transcript (AAV-hsyn, 30.8 ± 14.6%, P=0.0681) and PTBP1 protein levels (AAV-hsyn, 22.1 ± 6.4%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Downregulation of Ptbp1 transcript was 30.8 ± 14.6% in striatum tissues of AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice.
claims.source: Analysis of striatum tissues isolated from AAV-ctrl- and AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice revealed base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site (AAV-ctrl, 0.4 ± 0.1%; AAV-hsyn, 23.0 ± 6.6%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and downregulation of Ptbp1 transcript (AAV-hsyn, 30.8 ± 14.6%, P=0.0681) and PTBP1 protein levels (AAV-hsyn, 22.1 ± 6.4%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Virtually all TH+ cells in the intact SNc were co-stained for NEUN (99.0 ± 0.1%).
claims.source: As expected, virtually all TH+ cells in the intact SNc were co-stained for NEUN (99.0 ± 0.1%; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The majority of TH+ cells in the lesioned SNc (92.0 ± 6.2%) and striatum (77.5 ± 11.8%) of AAV-hsyn-treated animals were labeled by NEUN.
claims.source: Likewise, the majority of TH+ cells in the lesioned SNc (hsyn: 92.0 ± 6.2%; Figure 3B) and striatum of AAV-hsyn-treated animals (77.5 ± 11.8%; Figure 3C) were also labeled by NEUN, further corroborating a neuronal origin of these cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: A significant reduction in the surface area and Feret's diameter was observed between TH/NEUN double-positive cells in the lesioned striatum compared to endogenous DANs in the intact SNc.
claims.source: Moreover, we observed a significant reduction in the surface area (p<0.0001) and Feret's diameter (p<0.0001) between TH/NEUN double-positive cells in the lesioned striatum compared to endogenous DANs in the intact SNc, or TH/NEUN double-positive cell bodies in the lesioned SNc of AAV-hsyn-treated mice (Figure 3D; surface area, p<0.001; Feret's diameter, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Injection of AAV-hsyn into the visual cortex did not lead to TH expression in local neurons.
claims.source: In line with previous work (Qian et al., 2020), injection of AAV-hsyn into the visual cortex did not lead to TH expression in local neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 5; n=174 Cas9/NEUN double-positive cells), suggesting that the local microenvironment indeed plays a contributing role in inducing TH expression in the targeted neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and a citation to Qian et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Microscopic analysis of 163 TH/NEUN double-positive cells revealed no co-labeling with BrdU.
claims.source: Microscopic analysis of 163 TH/NEUN double-positive cells revealed no co-labeling with BrdU (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), indicating that TH+ cells were not generated de novo and rather originated from non-proliferating mature neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: TH+ cells were not generated de novo and rather originated from non-proliferating mature neurons.
claims.source: Microscopic analysis of 163 TH/NEUN double-positive cells revealed no co-labeling with BrdU (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), indicating that TH+ cells were not generated de novo and rather originated from non-proliferating mature neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of BrdU labeling in TH/NEUN double-positive cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: The majority of TH+ cells also expressed the marker DAT (75.2 ± 5.6%).
claims.source: The majority of TH+ cells also expressed the marker DAT (75.2 ± 5.6%; Figure 4A and B), further corroborating the DA identity of these cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Only a small fraction of TH/DAT double-positive cells were labeled for markers of neural progenitors (SOX2, 9.1 ± 2.4%; NESTIN, 2.1 ± 0.5%; DCX, 2.6 ± 0.8%).
claims.source: Moreover, supporting the results of our BrdU-labeling experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), only a small fraction of TH/DAT double-positive cells were labeled for markers of neural progenitors (SOX2, 9.1 ± 2.4%; NESTIN, 2.1 ± 0.5%; DCX, 2.6 ± 0.8%; Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Most TH/DAT-labeled cells expressed the adult pan-neuronal marker NEUN (86.2 ± 3.7%).
claims.source: Instead, most TH/DAT-labeled cells expressed the adult pan-neuronal marker NEUN (86.2 ± 3.7%; Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Of the TH/DAT/NEUN-positive population, 49.8 ± 12.9% were additionally labeled with CTIP2, a marker for GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs).
claims.source: Of this TH/DAT/NEUN-positive population, 49.8 ± 12.9% were additionally labeled with CTIP2 (Figure 4A and B), a marker for GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs), and 46.4 ± 10.4% expressed markers for various GABAergic interneurons (PV, 3.2 ± 1.9%; SST, 3.5 ± 1.2%; CALB2, 39.7 ± 11.0%; Figure 4A and B), indicating that expression of DA markers may be achieved in various subtypes of GABAergic neurons upon PTBP1 downregulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: 46.4 ± 10.4% of TH/DAT/NEUN-positive cells expressed markers for various GABAergic interneurons (PV, 3.2 ± 1.9%; SST, 3.5 ± 1.2%; CALB2, 39.7 ± 11.0%).
claims.source: Of this TH/DAT/NEUN-positive population, 49.8 ± 12.9% were additionally labeled with CTIP2 (Figure 4A and B), a marker for GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs), and 46.4 ± 10.4% expressed markers for various GABAergic interneurons (PV, 3.2 ± 1.9%; SST, 3.5 ± 1.2%; CALB2, 39.7 ± 11.0%; Figure 4A and B), indicating that expression of DA markers may be achieved in various subtypes of GABAergic neurons upon PTBP1 downregulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Expression of DA markers may be achieved in various subtypes of GABAergic neurons upon PTBP1 downregulation.
claims.source: Of this TH/DAT/NEUN-positive population, 49.8 ± 12.9% were additionally labeled with CTIP2 (Figure 4A and B), a marker for GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs), and 46.4 ± 10.4% expressed markers for various GABAergic interneurons (PV, 3.2 ± 1.9%; SST, 3.5 ± 1.2%; CALB2, 39.7 ± 11.0%; Figure 4A and B), indicating that expression of DA markers may be achieved in various subtypes of GABAergic neurons upon PTBP1 downregulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the 4i imaging data showing expression of GABAergic markers in TH/DAT/NEUN-positive cells in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Drug-free motor dysfunctions were significantly alleviated in animals treated with AAV-hsyn in the SNc.
claims.source: We found that drug-free motor dysfunctions were significantly alleviated in animals treated with AAV-hsyn (stepping test, p<0.0001; cylinder test, p<0.0001), but not with AAV-GFAP (stepping test, p=0.8608; cylinder test, p=0.0504), in the SNc when using an AAV dose of 2×108 vg per animal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Drug-free motor dysfunctions were not significantly alleviated in animals treated with AAV-GFAP in the SNc.
claims.source: We found that drug-free motor dysfunctions were significantly alleviated in animals treated with AAV-hsyn (stepping test, p<0.0001; cylinder test, p<0.0001), but not with AAV-GFAP (stepping test, p=0.8608; cylinder test, p=0.0504), in the SNc when using an AAV dose of 2×108 vg per animal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: PTBP1 targeting in striatal neurons restored the asymmetry of spontaneous behaviors.
claims.source: Likewise, PTBP1 targeting in striatal neurons restored the asymmetry of spontaneous behaviors (AAV-hsyn: stepping test, p<0.0001; cylinder test, p<0.0001; AAV-ctrl: stepping test, p=0.2667; cylinder test, p=0.1870; Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: No recovery of contralateral rotations was detected in treated animals after systemic administration of amphetamine.
claims.source: However, we did not detect recovery of contralateral rotations in treated animals after systemic administration of amphetamine (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which leads to an enhanced imbalance of extracellular dopamine concentrations between the denervated and intact striatum (Freyberg et al., 2016; Karam et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: No recovery of ipsilateral rotations was observed in any treatment group after systemic administration of apomorphine.
claims.source: Likewise, after systemic administration of apomorphine, which acts as a dopamine receptor agonist and stimulates hypersensitive dopamine receptors in the lesioned hemisphere (Arroyo-García et al., 2018; da Conceição et al., 2010; Iancu et al., 2005), we did not observe a recovery of ipsilateral rotations in any treatment group (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Delivery of dual AAV vectors to the SNc resulted in the formation of TH-expressing cells and the rescue of spontaneous behaviors when a neuronal promoter was used to drive ABE expression.
claims.source: Delivery of dual AAV vectors to the SNc resulted in the formation of TH-expressing cells and the rescue of spontaneous behaviors when a neuronal promoter was used to drive ABE expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claims.claim: No DA projections to the striatum were detected following neuronal PTBP1 downregulation in the SNc.
claims.source: However, no DA projections to the striatum were detected, supporting recent findings that suggest a functional role of PTBP1 in promoting axon regeneration of adult sensory neurons (Alber et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2E and F and a citation to Alber et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Reconstitution of the nigrostriatal pathway is unlikely the mechanism underlying the observed phenotypic rescue.
claims.source: Reconstitution of the nigrostriatal pathway, which connects the SNc with the dorsal striatum (Kalia and Lang, 2015), is therefore unlikely the mechanism underlying the observed phenotypic rescue.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of DA projections to the striatum despite behavioral improvements.

claims.claim: The downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 in the striatum of 6-OHDA-lesioned mice led to the formation of TH+ cells and a rescue of spontaneous behaviors.
claims.source: Supporting this hypothesis, the downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 in the striatum of 6-OHDA-lesioned mice also led to the formation of TH+ cells and a rescue of spontaneous behaviors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claims.claim: The study contributes to evidence indicating that downregulation of astroglial PTBP1 does not induce astrocyte conversion into DANs.
claims.source: Our study contributes to this recently growing body of evidence, indicating that downregulation of astroglial PTBP1 does not induce astrocyte conversion into DANs, and that neurons are the origin of the observed TH+ cells (Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and citations to Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Neurons are the origin of the observed TH+ cells.
claims.source: Our study contributes to this recently growing body of evidence, indicating that downregulation of astroglial PTBP1 does not induce astrocyte conversion into DANs, and that neurons are the origin of the observed TH+ cells (Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data showing NEUN co-labeling in TH+ cells and citations to Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023.

claims.claim: 4i and BrdU experiments revealed that TH expression in the striatum was induced in mature neurons, either expressing markers of GABAergic MSNs or interneurons.
claims.source: Our 4i and BrdU experiments furthermore revealed that TH expression in the striatum was induced in mature neurons, either expressing markers of GABAergic MSNs or interneurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: The interplay between microRNAs (miRNAs) and the RNA processing proteins PTBP1 and nPTBP is crucial during neuronal differentiation and maturation.
claims.source: Previous research has demonstrated that the interplay between microRNAs (miRNAs) and the RNA processing proteins PTBP1 and its homology nPTBP (PTBP2) is crucial during neuronal differentiation and maturation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Boutz et al., 2007; Makeyev et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boutz et al., 2007; Makeyev et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The activation of the PTBP1/nPTBP regulatory loops is essential for driving reprogramming toward the neuronal lineage and subsequent neuronal maturation.
claims.source: Thus, the activation of the PTBP1/nPTBP regulatory loops is essential for driving reprogramming toward the neuronal lineage and subsequent neuronal maturation (Xue et al., 2016; Xue et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xue et al., 2016; Xue et al., 2013.

claims.claim: PTBP1 is sufficiently expressed and plays a functional role in mature neurons.
claims.source: While this classical model of PTBP1 down-regulation and neuronal differentiation implies negligible expression or importance of PTBP1 in mature neurons, our results indicate that PTBP1 is sufficiently expressed and plays a functional role in mature neurons, with the installation of a loss-of-function mutation resulting in a detectable reduction in relative protein amounts (Figure 2—figure supplement 5; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and behavioral improvements in a PD mouse model (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing PTBP1 expression in mature neurons and behavioral improvements upon PTBP1 downregulation.

claims.claim: A recent study demonstrated PTBP1 expression in axons of sensory and motor neurons as well as a functional role in sensation, injury response, and axonal regeneration.
claims.source: Supporting these findings, a recent study demonstrated PTBP1 expression in axons of sensory and motor neurons as well as a functional role in sensation, injury response, and axonal regeneration (Alber et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alber et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Both MSNs and interneurons receive DA inputs from the SNc.
claims.source: Since both MSNs and interneurons receive DA inputs from the SNc, their activity, and excitability are strongly hampered when striatal dopamine is absent (Bamford et al., 2018; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bamford et al., 2018; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008.

claims.claim: PTBP1 downregulation by adenine base editing and subsequent TH expression might have enabled local dopamine synthesis in the dorsal striatum.
claims.source: It, therefore, seems feasible that PTBP1 downregulation by adenine base editing and subsequent TH expression might have enabled local dopamine synthesis in the dorsal striatum, which may have been sufficient to partly restore the function of these cell populations and compensate for the depletion of DA inputs from the SNc.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the observed TH expression and dopamine increase.

claims.claim: Depletion of GPR6 in D2-MSNs reduced intracellular cAMP concentrations, leading to increased striatal dopamine and decreased involuntary movements following apomorphine treatment in 6-OHDA-lesioned PD mice.

results.result: Adenine base editors (ABEs) effectively downregulate PTBP1 in cell lines through splice site disruption. ABEs enable gene editing without DNA double-strand breaks and achieve high editing rates (up to 92.9% in Hepa cells) at splice donor sites, resulting in substantial reduction of PTBP1 transcript and protein levels across multiple cell lines (Hepa, N2a, C8-D1A).
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C28 and C81-C82 are well-supported by sequencing data (Figure 1 and supplements), RT-qPCR, and Western blot analyses showing consistent PTBP1 downregulation across cell lines. The methodology is validated with appropriate controls and multiple independent experiments.

results.result: 6-OHDA successfully induced a severe unilateral lesion in the nigrostriatal pathway of mice, characterized by 99% reduction in TH+ dopaminergic neurons in the SNc, 92% decrease in striatal DA fibers, increased astrocyte activation, and significant motor deficits including ipsilateral rotations and contralateral forelimb akinesia.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by comprehensive histological quantification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and behavioral testing with appropriate statistical analysis. The PD model is well-characterized and consistent with cited literature.

results.result: PTBP1 downregulation in neurons, but not astrocytes, of the SNc generates TH-expressing cells in a PD mouse model. AAV-hsyn treatment resulted in restoration of approximately 10% of TH+ cells in the lesioned SNc with confirmed base editing (~15%) and PTBP1 reduction (~25%), while AAV-GFAP treatment showed no effect above control levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34, C4, C37-C38, C59, C63-C64 are supported by histological quantification (Figure 2), molecular validation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), and consistent with recent literature challenging astrocyte-to-neuron conversion. The cell-type specific effects are clearly demonstrated with appropriate promoters and controls.

results.result: TH+ cells generated in the SNc upon neuronal PTBP1 downregulation did not form striatal projections or restore the nigrostriatal pathway. No increase in DA fiber fluorescence was detected in the striatum or medial forebrain bundle despite the presence of TH+ cells in the SNc.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C60-C61 are supported by histological analysis (Figure 2E-F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) showing no significant differences in striatal DA projections between treatment groups. This finding is consistent with cited work on PTBP1's role in axon regeneration.

results.result: PTBP1 downregulation in striatal neurons generates TH-expressing cells and rescues motor behaviors. AAV-hsyn treatment in the striatum resulted in ~106 TH+ cells per 3 sections with 23% base editing and 31% PTBP1 transcript reduction, leading to TH expression in non-dividing neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41, C62, C5, C21 are supported by histological quantification (Figure 3A), molecular validation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and BrdU labeling experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 6). The data consistently demonstrate TH induction in striatal neurons.

results.result: TH+ cells in the striatum originate from mature, non-dividing neurons. The majority of TH+ cells co-express NEUN (77.5-92%) and show no BrdU labeling (0/163 cells analyzed), indicating they arise from post-mitotic neurons rather than proliferating progenitors. These cells are morphologically distinct from endogenous DANs.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47, C64-C65 are supported by immunohistochemistry (Figure 3B-C), BrdU labeling (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), and morphometric analysis (Figure 3D). The absence of BrdU labeling in all 163 TH/NEUN+ cells provides strong evidence against de novo neurogenesis.

results.result: TH+ cells in the striatum are mature GABAergic neurons expressing dopaminergic markers. Multiplexed 4i imaging revealed that 75.2% of TH+ cells express DAT, 86.2% express NEUN, with minimal progenitor markers (<10%). Of TH/DAT/NEUN+ cells, 49.8% are GABAergic MSNs (CTIP2+) and 46.4% are GABAergic interneurons (PV/SST/CALB2+).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53, C8-C9 are supported by comprehensive 4i imaging data (Figure 4) with validated antibodies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The phenotypic characterization is thorough and demonstrates that TH expression occurs in multiple GABAergic neuronal subtypes.

results.result: PTBP1 downregulation in striatal neurons increases dopamine levels. AAV-hsyn-treated mice showed a 2.5-fold increase in striatal dopamine (4.4±2.6 vs 1.7±0.7 nmol/g protein, p=0.0159) and increased DOPAC (8.2±3.9 vs 3.1±1.8 nmol/g protein, p=0.0449) in the lesioned hemisphere.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80, C6, C73 are supported by HPLC quantification (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) with appropriate controls and statistical analysis. The dopamine increase is modest but statistically significant and correlates with TH expression.

results.result: Neuronal PTBP1 downregulation alleviates spontaneous motor dysfunctions in PD mice. AAV-hsyn treatment significantly improved forelimb akinesia (p<0.0001) and spontaneous rotations (p<0.0001) in both SNc and striatum, while AAV-GFAP treatment showed no significant effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56, C7, C20 are supported by behavioral testing data (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical analysis and controls. The cell-type specific behavioral rescue is consistent with the histological findings.

results.result: PTBP1 downregulation does not rescue drug-induced motor behaviors. No recovery was observed in amphetamine-induced contralateral rotations or apomorphine-induced ipsilateral rotations in any treatment group, suggesting insufficient dopamine levels to reverse receptor hypersensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58, C77-C78 are supported by behavioral testing data (Figure 5C-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The lack of drug-induced behavioral rescue is consistent with the modest dopamine increase and absence of nigrostriatal pathway reconstruction.

results.result: Off-target editing is minimal and does not contribute to TH expression. GUIDE-seq identified two off-target sites (Mypn and Ank1) with substantially lower editing rates (5.4-5.8%) than the on-target Ptbp1 site (23.0%), and no reduction in off-target gene transcript levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are supported by GUIDE-seq analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and RT-qPCR validation. The comprehensive off-target analysis strengthens the conclusion that TH expression results from PTBP1 downregulation rather than off-target effects.

results.result: The local microenvironment contributes to TH expression induction. AAV-hsyn injection into the visual cortex did not induce TH expression in local neurons (0/174 Cas9/NEUN+ cells), suggesting region-specific factors are required.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by negative control experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and consistent with cited literature. However, the mechanism of microenvironmental influence remains unclear and requires further investigation.

results.result: PTBP1 is functionally expressed in mature neurons. Despite classical models suggesting negligible PTBP1 in mature neurons, loss-of-function mutations result in detectable protein reduction and behavioral improvements in PD mice, supported by recent findings of PTBP1 in axons of sensory and motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) showing PTBP1 expression in mature neurons and behavioral improvements upon downregulation. This challenges classical models and is corroborated by cited literature.

results.result: Local dopamine synthesis in striatal neurons may compensate for loss of SNc inputs. The authors propose that TH expression enabled local dopamine synthesis sufficient to restore function of MSNs and interneurons, with even modest dopamine increases rescuing spontaneous motor behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C74-C75 are speculative inferences from the observed TH expression, dopamine increase, and behavioral improvements. While the hypothesis is plausible and supported by cited work (Delignat-Lavaud et al., 2023), direct evidence of local dopamine synthesis and release from TH+ neurons is lacking. Microdialysis or fiber photometry would be needed to confirm.

results.result: The manuscript contextualizes findings within established knowledge of PTBP1/nPTBP regulatory loops in neuronal differentiation, striatal circuitry, and dopamine-dependent motor control, citing appropriate literature to support the mechanistic framework.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67, C70, C72, C76 accurately represent cited literature and established knowledge. These provide appropriate context for interpreting the experimental findings.

results.result: The manuscript accurately describes established knowledge about Parkinson's disease pathology, current treatment limitations, and the role of tyrosine hydroxylase in dopamine synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C11, C22-C23 accurately represent well-established knowledge about PD and are appropriately cited. These provide necessary background context.

results.result: The manuscript accurately summarizes prior controversial work on PTBP1-mediated astrocyte-to-neuron conversion and subsequent studies questioning this model, providing appropriate context for the current investigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C15-C17 accurately represent cited prior work (Qian et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Hoang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021) and frame the scientific controversy appropriately.

results.result: The manuscript accurately describes properties of astrocytes relevant to cell fate switching approaches, including their resistance to neurodegeneration, multipotency when activated, and proliferative capacity in brain injuries.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14 accurately represent cited literature about astrocyte properties and provide rationale for targeting these cells in regenerative approaches.

results.result: The authors developed an adenine base editing (ABE) strategy to disrupt the Ptbp1 splice site, achieving efficient editing rates (64-93%) in multiple cell lines, resulting in substantial reduction of PTBP1 protein levels without generating functional protein from alternative splice sites.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the ABE strategy as 'sound' and 'interesting,' with one reviewer noting it is 'potentially more therapeutically relevant than previous approaches.' The methodology is accepted without critique, and the editor states the approach has 'clear implications for Parkinson's disease therapeutics.'

results.result: PTBP1 downregulation in astrocytes using AAV-GFAP had no effect on TH+ cell formation or motor function rescue in the 6-OHDA PD model, while neurons are the origin of observed TH+ cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding, with one stating the manuscript 'adds to the growing literature challenging previous findings' about astrocyte conversion. Another reviewer notes the study 'effectively counteracts previous work in line with more recent publications,' and the editor confirms the study 'addresses recent controversial literature on cell reprogramming.'

results.result: PTBP1 downregulation in neurons of the SNc and striatum resulted in the expression of TH in non-dividing neurons, with approximately 10% restoration of TH+ cells in the SNc and ~2,646 cells in the striatum, with the majority co-expressing the neuronal marker NEUN.
results.evaluation: The editor states that 'neuron-specific loss of function of the RNA splicing factor Ptbp1 in striatal neurons induces dopaminergic markers,' describing the evidence as 'solid.' Reviewers accept these findings without challenge, though one notes 'additional characterization of dopaminergic neuronal identity may be required in future studies.'

results.result: Multiplexed 4i imaging revealed that most TH+ cells co-expressed DAT (75.2%) and NEUN (86.2%), with the majority classified as mature GABAergic neurons (MSNs: 49.8%; interneurons: 46.4%), and only a small fraction expressing neural progenitor markers.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the immunohistochemical data, one explicitly states 'the identity of the converted neurons is unclear' and notes that 'though the immunohistochemical methodology indicates they may be MSNs and/or interneurons, a more comprehensive identity is still lacking.' The editor echoes this, stating 'additional characterization of dopaminergic neuronal identity may be required in future studies.'

results.result: BrdU labeling experiments showed that TH/NEUN double-positive cells (n=163) did not co-label with BrdU, indicating TH+ cells originated from non-proliferating mature neurons rather than being generated de novo.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. The data directly supports the neuronal origin claim, which reviewers explicitly endorse as part of the manuscript's contribution to 'challenging previous findings' about cell conversion mechanisms.

results.result: PTBP1 downregulation in striatal neurons was associated with a 2.5-fold increase in striatal dopamine concentrations (4.4±2.6 vs 1.7±0.7 nmol/g protein) and increased DOPAC levels, as measured by HPLC.
results.evaluation: One reviewer expresses concern that 'striatal dopamine was assessed by whole-tissue analysis, which is not necessarily reflective of synaptic dopamine availability,' making it 'difficult to assess whether the ~10% increase in TH+ cells in the striatum was sufficient to improve dopamine function.' However, the reviewer acknowledges 'the improvement in motor activity suggests that it was,' indicating mixed evaluation of the dopamine measurement's functional significance.

results.result: PTBP1 downregulation in striatal neurons rescued spontaneous motor behaviors including forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations in the 6-OHDA PD model.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states 'the evidence supporting the rescue of motor deficits following Ptbp1 manipulation is solid.' Reviewers accept the behavioral improvements, with one noting that despite uncertainty about dopamine measurements, 'the improvement in motor activity suggests' functional restoration occurred.

results.result: No recovery of drug-induced rotational behaviors was observed after amphetamine or apomorphine administration in AAV-hsyn-treated animals, indicating insufficient dopamine levels to normalize responses to dopaminomimetic drugs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. One reviewer notes the treatment was 'insufficient to normalize responses to dopaminomimetic drugs,' acknowledging this limitation while still supporting the overall therapeutic potential of the approach.

results.result: TH+ cells generated in the SNc upon neuronal PTBP1 downregulation did not form striatal projections, as evidenced by lack of increased DA fiber fluorescence in the striatum and medial forebrain bundle, suggesting reconstitution of the nigrostriatal pathway is unlikely the mechanism of phenotypic rescue.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. The data showing lack of striatal projections is consistent with the authors' conclusion that behavioral improvements must result from local striatal dopamine production rather than pathway reconstitution.

results.result: 6-OHDA induced a severe unilateral lesion characterized by 99% reduction in SNc TH+ neurons, 92% decrease in striatal DA fibers, increased GFAP+ astrocytes, and significantly increased ipsilateral rotations and contralateral forelimb akinesia.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the lesion characterization data, one explicitly critiques the model choice, stating 'the 6-OHDA model, though useful to examine dopaminergic cell loss, exhibits accelerated neurodegeneration and none of the typical pathological hallmarks (synucleinopathy, Lewy bodies, etc.) compared to the typical etiology of Parkinson disease, limiting its translational interpretation.'

results.result: GUIDE-seq analysis identified two off-target sites (Mypn and Ank1 genes) with substantially lower editing rates (5.4-5.8%) than the Ptbp1 target site (23.0%), and no reduction in transcript levels of these genes, indicating TH induction is likely a direct consequence of PTBP1 downregulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the off-target analysis without challenge. The comprehensive assessment of specificity supports the conclusion that observed effects are on-target, which is consistent with reviewers' overall acceptance of the ABE strategy as sound.

results.result: The authors propose that PTBP1 is functionally expressed in mature neurons and that its downregulation enables local dopamine synthesis in the striatum, establishing a basal tone of extracellular dopamine sufficient to rescue spontaneous motor behaviors despite modest increases in dopamine levels.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic interpretation is not directly evaluated by reviewers. One reviewer notes 'there remains no real evidence that these cells actually release dopamine,' highlighting uncertainty about the functional mechanism. The speculative nature of claims C71 and C74 (marked as 'INFERENCE' and 'SPECULATION' in evidence) suggests reviewers would view this as requiring further validation.

results.result: Base editing and PTBP1 downregulation were confirmed in both SNc (14.7-15.5% editing; 23.7-24.8% transcript reduction) and striatum (23.0% editing; 30.8% transcript reduction) tissues at experimental endpoints.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these molecular validation data without challenge. The confirmation of on-target editing and knockdown supports the overall experimental design and interpretation.

results.result: TH/NEUN double-positive cells in the lesioned striatum showed significantly reduced cell surface area and diameter compared to endogenous DANs in the intact SNc, and injection of AAV-hsyn into the visual cortex did not induce TH expression, suggesting the local microenvironment plays a role in TH induction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these morphological and regional specificity findings without challenge. The data support the conclusion that TH induction is context-dependent and that the generated cells differ morphologically from endogenous dopaminergic neurons.
